transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-14 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (VentureLoop Head of Platform), Tom Nguyen (Network), Riley Brooks (Security), Samir Bose (SRE)

Summary:
Quick discovery to validate VentureLoop's private onramp requirements for Redwood Private (VPC) — focus on latency SLOs for customer-facing inference, egress restrictions (company uses outbound proxy + strict egress IP allowlist), regional residency constraints (EU-only for some traffic), and whether PrivateLink (Private endpoints) or TGW/VPC peering is best fit. Also discussed SOC2, SSO/KMS, and sample network handoff items.

Topics:
- Latency SLOs and network topology (direct vs transit gateway)
- Egress and NAT / proxy constraints
- Private endpoint vs peering tradeoffs
- Region gating and data residency
- Security: KMS/HSM, audit logs, SSO, RBAC

Action items (short): Jordan to send security packet & checklist; Maya to prepare network diagram; Tom to share VPC ranges and egress details.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. Maya's here from solutions to do the tech bits. How's everybody doing?
[00:12] Asha: Good, thanks. We wanted to get into the networking constraints first — we've got a pretty locked-down egress policy and a couple of regional constraints.
[00:20] Maya: Great. Quick question up front — are you leaning Hosted or Private? I saw in the intake that you're evaluating Private for data residency and isolation reasons?
[00:29] Asha: Yeah, the shorthand is we need private. We have EU-only processing for some endpoints, and the team wants control of the egress IPs so we can allowlist them in partner systems.
[00:40] Samir: Also latency. Our user-facing features have a p50 p90 SLO — basically 100ms p50 and 250ms p90 end-to-end from our app to inference response in the EU region.
[00:52] Jordan: Okay that's helpful. We typically see with Redwood Private you can meet those numbers with colocated capacity in the same region, but network path matters — are you using a transit gateway, peering, or PrivateLink today to connect 3rd parties into your VPCs?
[01:05] Tom: We use a TGW for cross-account routing internally, and most external services go through our outbound proxy — squid-based — so everything egresses from NATs with fixed IPs.
[01:16] Riley: From security side we need to ensure any private endpoint IPs are documented — and if Redwood hosts an endpoint in our VPC we'll need mutual TLS and audit logs.
[01:26] Maya: Notes: mutual TLS for private endpoints is doable, and we can emit audit logs to your SIEM via our console integrations. We'll confirm log retention options.
[01:35] Asha: One wrinkle: we have a partner that only allows traffic from a small set of egress IPs. We can't have dynamic ephemeral egress IPs there.
[01:45] Jordan: Right, so two approaches: 1) Redwood Private deployed into your VPC via a PrivateLink endpoint — traffic stays in your network and egress is controlled entirely by you; or 2) dedicated Redwood-hosted capacity in our VPC but with static NAT egress IPs published for allowlisting and a peering/TGW to route traffic. Each has tradeoffs on latency and operational overhead.
[02:05] Tom: If we do PrivateLink, who manages the endpoint and certificates? Also, do you support interface endpoints in multiple AZs?
[02:14] Maya: For PrivateLink we provide the service name and you create the interface endpoints in your VPC. Certificates for the mTLS can be customer-managed or we can terminate with Redwood-managed certs — if you need client certs from your side we can accept them. We recommend creating endpoints in at least two AZs for HA.
[02:30] Samir: Does PrivateLink add noticeable latency? Our perf team is sensitive to any extra hop.
[02:36] Maya: Usually the added serialization is minimal — sub 5–10ms typically inside a single region for interface endpoints. The bigger latency factors are whether requests need to traverse proxy/NAT and any extra hops to a shared TGW.
[02:49] Asha: Our architecture today routes everything through an egress proxy which does TLS inspection — so we can't just bypass it. We need to see how Redwood fits into that path.
[02:58] Jordan: Understood. One pattern we've seen: deploy Redwood Private in a dedicated account connected to your TGW, then set a route so calls to Redwood service IPs traverse your proxy/NAT as normal. Alternatively, add an interface endpoint in the app VPC and keep egress control local — depends on whether you prefer full control of egress IPs.
[03:16] Riley: From security point, we also need KMS integration. Keys must be customer-managed for production in our EU tenant. Do you support bringing your own KMS/HSM?
[03:25] Maya: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest. For HSM-backed keys we have an integration pattern that plugs into major cloud KMS providers; we'll send the details in the security packet. There is a small ops step to provision access with the right IAM roles.
[03:38] Tom: And audit logs — we need requests and response metadata for compliance. How granular are your logs? We can't store raw PII but we do need trace ids, timestamps, and token counts for billing reconciliation.
[03:51] Jordan: Our Console can export audit logs with request IDs, model version, latency, token counts, and trace flags — contents can be redacted. We'll include sample log format in the packet.
[04:03] Asha: Great. Next — region gating. We have EU-only workloads that must not cross into US regions. If Redwood's control plane is global, how do we ensure data paths remain EU-only?
[04:15] Maya: Redwood Private has a customer-controlled dataplane for Private deployments — the inference nodes and KV cache can be pinned to specific regions. The control plane can be your private control plane (Private option) so the orchestration stays in your region. We can also provide a hosted control plane with region restrictions, but for strict data residency we recommend Private control plane.
[04:36] Samir: So if we pin to eu-west-1, everything stays inside that region including KV cache?
[04:41] Maya: Yes, inference, KV cache, and model weights are placed in that region. Only control messages (if using Redwood hosted control plane) may transit to our service unless you opt for Private control plane. We'll add the architecture note to the diagram.
[04:52] Tom: On network ports — what ports do we need to open? Is it HTTPS only?
[04:57] Maya: HTTPS (443) is the primary, and mTLS uses TLS over 443. For healthchecks and metrics we usually use 8080 internally but that doesn't need to be public. We'll include a port list in the handoff doc.
[05:09] Riley: Are there any restrictions on throughput? We have bursts up to 200 QPS during peak campaigns and token throughput is variable.
[05:16] Maya: We size GPU pools to meet throughput; for Private deployments you can reserve dedicated capacity with burst options. For the network, the main limit is egress bandwidth from your NAT/proxy — you should allow enough bandwidth and low jitter for steady p90 latency. We'll include a recommended bandwidth per QPS figure in the follow-up.
[05:32] Asha: One more thing — our downstream partner requires a fixed source IP for webhooks. If Redwood is in our VPC via PrivateLink that solves it, but if Redwood is hosted we need static egress IPs published. What's your published egress IP policy?
[05:46] Jordan: For dedicated-hosted we can provide static egress IPs for enterprise customers on Dedicated. For hosted multitenant, egress IPs can change. For Private we can leave egress entirely under your control.
[05:58] Tom: Good to know. Also curious about fallback and high availability — if a region has capacity shortages, can Redwood failover to another region while preserving compliance?
[06:07] Maya: We have automatic fallback policies but for strict residency you'd disable cross-region fallback. Instead we'd do a canary or queued requests with a fail-open policy only if you allow cross-region.
[06:19] Samir: And latency if we must failover? Probably not acceptable for these EU-only flows; we'd prefer queued or degrade gracefully.
[06:27] Jordan: Agreed. We can set a route that rejects cross-region calls and surface an explicit error to the app so you'd handle fallback in-app.
[06:36] Asha: On the ops side, what's the onboarding timeline and what do you need from us to get a Private deployment started?
[06:44] Maya: Typical timeline: 2–4 weeks for initial setup assuming network details and certs are ready. Key things we need: VPC CIDRs, TGW IDs or peering info, egress NAT IPs or proxy config, SAML metadata for SSO if you want console access, and the list of IAM roles we'll use during setup.
[07:00] Tom: We'll need a one-pager on the exact steps. Also, we use a proxy for TLS inspection — will the Redwood agent be able to talk through it?
[07:08] Maya: Yes, the agent can communicate through HTTP(S) proxies; we'll document the proxy auth options and any timeouts to watch for.
[07:17] Riley: About SSO — we use SAML 2.0 and expect RBAC mapping back to our IdP groups. Can Redwood map roles from SAML assertions?
[07:25] Jordan: Yes, we support SAML and SCIM for user provisioning and can map group attributes to RBAC roles. We'll include a sample mapping in the security packet.
[07:33] Asha: Are there any additional compliance artifacts we should expect? Pen test, SOC2, iso?
[07:39] Jordan: We can share SOC2 Type II and our standard pen test summary; for ISO we have a roadmap and can discuss enterprise packages.
[07:47] Tom: Network routing question — if we call out to Redwood from our app VPC over PrivateLink, do we still require NAT egress for outbound model calls or is it strictly inbound to the endpoint?
[07:58] Maya: With interface endpoints, traffic to Redwood is directly to the endpoint — no NAT egress required for that traffic. Outbound to external partners from Redwood (if your model has webhooks) will egress from your VPC if endpoints are configured and routes are set to keep traffic local.
[08:12] Samir: We do use webhooks to a partner in EU; need to ensure source IP is consistent.
[08:17] Jordan: That aligns — PrivateLink keeps source IP inside your VPC. We'll confirm in the diagram.
[08:22] Asha: One more: billing and token logs — we need reconciliation fields so our finance team can map calls back to internal request IDs.
[08:29] Jordan: We can add a request_id header that you pass and we echo in logs; that helps reconciliation. We'll show sample logs.
[08:37] Tom: What about KV cache locality — if the cache is in a different AZ could that increase tail latency?
[08:44] Maya: Yes, ideally KV cache should be collocated in same AZ or region to keep tail latency down. For high availability we replicate across AZs but read/write locality matters. We'll include recommendations for cache placement and cache TTL to avoid repeated fetches.
[08:59] Riley: Any special firewall rules for health checks or metrics that our security team needs to allow?
[09:04] Maya: Healthchecks run on the internal metrics port but typically over private network, not public. We'll list CIDRs, ports, and HTTPS endpoints in the handoff doc.
[09:13] Asha: Ok, let's talk slightly about tradeoffs: PrivateLink in our VPC sounds like the simplest for egress control, but we worry about the ops burden of maintaining endpoints across multiple accounts. If we have many accounts behind the TGW, peering to a dedicated account with Redwood might be easier.
[09:29] Jordan: Exactly. If you have many accounts trailing behind a TGW, creating a central Redwood-connected account and routing through TGW reduces endpoint sprawl but does introduce an extra hop which can add a few ms. There's also maintenance: PrivateLink endpoints are per VPC.
[09:42] Samir: So cost-wise is there a difference? Interface endpoints have per-hour charges, TGW has transit costs, and dedicated-hosted will have Redwood egress published, right?
[09:51] Maya: Yep. We'll put a cost comparison: endpoint-hour costs, TGW data charges, and any Redwood-dedicated egress fees. For high QPS bare-metal or reserved capacity often wins on unit cost, but network costs can dominate depending on architecture.
[10:07] Asha: Alright, that's helpful. Anything about encryption in transit at token level? We want TLS 1.2+ and perfect forward secrecy.
[10:15] Maya: We support TLS 1.2 and 1.3; for sensitive workloads we recommend 1.3 and client certificates. Key rotation can be customer-managed via KMS.
[10:24] Tom: Could you briefly outline what you'd like from us as immediate next steps?
[10:29] Jordan: Sure: we'll send a security packet, a short network-handshake checklist, and a draft diagram showing two patterns: PrivateLink per-VPC and TGW-centralized routing with allowed egress. Then schedule a 45-minute technical deep-dive for next week.
[10:44] Asha: Sounds good. One last question: do you support bringing models into our private deployment or do we have to use the models hosted by Redwood?
[10:52] Maya: We support onboarding custom customer models for Private deployments if they meet the runtime constraints; there's a model-ops step and we can run validation. For most customers we also recommend starting with a validated open model from our catalog to reduce ramp time.
[11:05] Riley: If we bring our own model, how are weights stored and who has access?
[11:10] Maya: We can store weights in your S3/GCS behind your KMS, or in our internal storage with customer-managed encryption. Access is restricted to the customer account and the nodes serving your requests. We'll include the model-onboarding checklist.
[11:22] Samir: Anything else about throttling? We need to set QPS limits per route to protect GPUs.
[11:28] Jordan: We can enforce per-route quotas and token rate limits. Also recommend a concurrency policy and burst buffers.
[11:36] Tom: Ok we'll gather the VPC info and send it.
[11:40] Asha: Thanks — this was very helpful.
[11:43] Jordan: Great. We'll recap next steps now.
